question: Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, what is the principal statutory duty of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI)?

C-O3.answer:
Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, the principal statutory duty of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is to **regulate and monitor the manufacture, processing, distribution, sale, and import of food so as to ensure safe and wholesome food** [23].

This duty is explicitly stated in Section 16(1) of the Act, which mandates that it shall be the duty of the Food Authority to regulate and monitor these activities for the purpose of ensuring food safety and wholesomeness [23].

While Section 16 outlines additional functions and powers, including the authority to specify regulations on food standards, additive limits, accreditation procedures, and international cooperation [24]-[33], the core statutory obligation remains the regulation and monitoring of the food supply chain to ensure safety [23].

The answer is based solely on the provided context, specifically Section 16(1) of the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 [23].

D2.answer: Under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, the principal statutory duty of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) is to regulate and monitor the manufacture, processing, distribution, sale and import of food so as to ensure safe and wholesome food [23].

D3.answer:
The principal statutory duty of the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 is to regulate and monitor the manufacture, processing, distribution, sale and import of food so as to ensure safe and wholesome food, as mandated by Section 16(1).

Sources: [22] [23]

question: Under the FSS Act 2006, what is the general licensing requirement for a person carrying on a food business?

C-O3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, Section 31(1) states that **no person shall commence or carry on any food business except under a licence** [25].

However, this requirement does not apply to certain categories of food business operators, namely:
- Petty manufacturers who themselves manufacture or sell any article of food
- Petty retailers, hawks, itinerant vendors, temporary stall holders
- Small scale or cottage or tiny food business operators

These exempted persons are required to **register themselves** with the appropriate authority in the manner specified by regulations [26].

The application for a licence must be made to the Designated Officer in the prescribed manner, containing the required particulars and fees [27].

D2.answer: Under Section 31(1) of the FSS Act 2006, no person shall commence or carry on any food business except under a licence [25]. However, this general requirement does not apply to petty manufacturers, retailers, hawkers, itinerant vendors, temporary stall holders, or small/cottage/tiny food business operators, who must instead register themselves with the appropriate authority as per Section 31(2) [26]. Applications for licences must be made to the Designated Officer with specified particulars and fees [27].

D3.answer:
Under Section 31(1) of the FSS Act 2006, the general licensing requirement is that no person shall commence or carry on any food business except under a licence. However, this requirement does not apply to petty manufacturers, retailers, hawkers, itinerant vendors, temporary stall holders, or small/cottage/tiny food business operators, who must instead register themselves with the appropriate authority as per Section 31(2).

question: Under the FSS Act 2006, what is the fundamental responsibility of a food business operator concerning the food it handles?

C-O3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, the fundamental responsibility of a food business operator is to ensure that the articles of food satisfy the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder at all stages of production, processing, import, distribution and sale within the businesses under his control [35].

Additionally, no food business operator shall himself or through any person on his behalf manufacture, store, sell or distribute any article of food that is unsafe, misbranded, sub-standard, contains extraneous matter, requires a licence but is handled without one, is prohibited by the Food Authority or government, or is in contravention of any provision of the Act or its rules and regulations [36][37][38][39].

The operator must also not employ any person suffering from infectious, contagious or loathsome disease [40], and must provide a written guarantee about the nature and quality of food sold to vendors in the specified form [41].

If any unsafe food is part of a batch, lot or consignment, it is presumed that all food in that batch is also unsafe unless proven otherwise through detailed assessment [42].

D2.answer: Under Section 26(1) of the FSS Act 2006, the fundamental responsibility of a food business operator is to ensure that articles of food satisfy the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder at all stages of production, processing, import, distribution and sale within the businesses under its control [Source 35]. This duty is reinforced by Section 26(2), which prohibits the operator from manufacturing, storing, selling or distributing any article of food that is unsafe, misbranded, sub-standard, contains extraneous matter, lacks required licensing, or is prohibited by the Food Authority or government [Sources 36, 37, 38, 39].

D3.answer:
Under Section 26(1) of the FSS Act 2006, the fundamental responsibility of a food business operator is to ensure that articles of food satisfy the requirements of the Act and the rules and regulations made thereunder at all stages of production, processing, import, distribution and sale within the businesses under its control. This duty is supplemented by the prohibitions in Section 26(2) against handling unsafe, misbranded, sub-standard, unlicensed or prohibited food.
Caveats: The exact scope of 'businesses under his control' is not elaborated in the provided evidence.; The definition of 'food business operator' is not provided in the evidence..

question: Under Section 22 of the FSS Act 2006, how are the standards for articles of food established?

C-O3.answer:
Based on the provided context, the answer to how standards for articles of food are established under Section 22 of the FSS Act 2006 is:

**Section 22 of the FSS Act 2006 does not establish standards for articles of food.** Instead, it prohibits certain categories of food products unless standards are specified under the Act and regulations made thereunder. Specifically, Section 22 states that no person shall manufacture, distribute, sell, or import any novel food, genetically modified articles of food, irradiated food, organic foods, foods for special dietary uses, functional foods, neutraceuticals, health supplements, proprietary foods, and such other articles of food which the Central Government may notify in this behalf [17].

The section defines various terms including "genetically engineered or modified food," "organic food," and "proprietary and novel food" [23][24][25], but the actual establishment of standards for these articles of food would be done through regulations made under the Act, as indicated by the phrase "Save as otherwise provided under this Act and regulations made thereunder" [17].

The provided context does not contain the specific mechanism or authority for how these standards are established beyond referencing that they are made through regulations under the Act.

D2.answer: Under Section 22 of the FSS Act 2006, standards for articles of food are established through specifications made under the Act and the regulations made thereunder [17]. For organic foods, standards are defined through specified organic production standards [24], while for proprietary and novel foods, the absence of specified standards is compensated by a safety requirement [25].

D3.answer:
Under Section 22 of the FSS Act 2006, standards for articles of food are established through specifications made under the Act and the regulations made thereunder. For organic foods, standards are defined through specified organic production standards, while for proprietary and novel foods, the absence of specified standards is compensated by a safety requirement.
Caveats: The exact mechanism or authority responsible for specifying standards under the Act and regulations is not detailed in the provided evidence.; The scope of 'such other articles of food which the Central Government may notify' is not elaborated in the evidence..

question: Who is the principal enforcement authority under the FSS Act 2006 at the State level, and what is that officer entitled to do?

C-O3.answer:
Based on the provided context, the answer is as follows:

**Principal Enforcement Authority at State Level:** The **Commissioner of Food Safety** is the principal enforcement authority under the FSS Act 2006 at the State level. [49]

**What the Officer is Entitled to Do:** The Commissioner of Food Safety is entitled to perform all or any of the following functions:
- Prohibit, in the interest of public health, the manufacture, storage, distribution or sale of any article of food, either in the whole of the State or any area or part thereof for such period, not exceeding one year, as may be specified in the order notified in the Official Gazette. [51]
- Carry out surveys of industrial units engaged in the manufacture or processing of food in the State to find out compliance by such units of the standards notified by the Food Authority. [52]
- Conduct or organise training programmes for personnel and different segments of the food chain for generating awareness on food safety. [53]
- Ensure efficient and uniform implementation of standards and other requirements, ensuring objectivity, accountability, practicability, transparency and credibility. [54]
- Sanction prosecution for offences punishable with imprisonment under the Act. [55]
- Perform such other functions as the State Government may, in consultation with the Food Authority, prescribe. [56]

Additionally, the Commissioner may delegate (subject to conditions) certain powers to subordinate officers, except the power to appoint Designated Officers, Food Safety Officers, and Food Analysts. [137]

D2.answer: Under the FSS Act 2006, the principal enforcement authority at the State level is the Commissioner of Food Safety, appointed by the State Government under Section 30(1) [49]. The Commissioner is entitled to perform functions including prohibiting the manufacture, storage, distribution or sale of any article of food in the interest of public health [51], carrying out surveys of industrial units for compliance with food safety standards [52], conducting or organising training programmes for personnel and the food chain [53], ensuring efficient and uniform implementation of standards with objectivity, accountability, practicability, transparency and credibility [54], sanctioning prosecution for offences punishable with imprisonment under the Act [55], and exercising the same powers as a Food Safety Officer as specified in the Act [48].

D3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, the principal enforcement authority at the State level is the Commissioner of Food Safety, appointed by the State Government under Section 30(1). The Commissioner is entitled to perform functions including prohibiting manufacture, storage, distribution or sale of food articles in the interest of public health, conducting surveys of food industrial units, organizing training programmes, ensuring efficient and uniform implementation of food safety standards, sanctioning prosecution for offences punishable with imprisonment, and exercising the same powers as a Food Safety Officer as per Section 30(6).

question: Under the FSS Act 2006, what procedural protections apply when a Food Safety Officer takes a food sample for analysis?

C-O3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, the procedural protections when a Food Safety Officer takes a food sample for analysis are as follows:

1. **Payment of Sample Cost**: The Food Safety Officer must pay the cost of the sample to the person from whom it is taken, calculated at the rate at which the article is usually sold to the public [38].

2. **Presence of Witnesses**: When taking a sample under clause (a) of sub-section (1), sub-section (2), sub-section (4), or sub-section (6), the Food Safety Officer must call one or more persons to be present at the time of taking action and obtain their signatures [43].

3. **Safe Custody of Seized Articles**: After taking a sample, if the article is kept in the safe custody of the food business operator, the officer may require the operator to execute a bond for a sum equal to the value of the article with one or more sureties [105].

4. **Sending Sample for Analysis**: The sample must be sent for analysis to a Food Analyst for the local area within which the sample was taken [36].

5. **Reporting Requirements**: The Food Analyst must submit the analysis report to the Designated Officer, including four copies indicating the method of sampling and analysis [48].

These provisions ensure transparency, accountability, and fairness in the sampling process while protecting the interests of food business operators.

D2.answer: Under Section 38 of the FSS Act 2006, when a Food Safety Officer takes a food sample for analysis, the procedural protections include: (1) payment of the sample cost to the person from whom it is taken at the usual public sale rate [38]; (2) calling one or more persons to be present and obtaining their signatures [43]; (3) giving written notice to the food business operator before destroying perishable food unfit for consumption [39]; and (4) following the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, as far as possible [40].

D3.answer:
Under Section 38 of the FSS Act 2006, when a Food Safety Officer takes a food sample for analysis, the procedural protections include: (1) payment of the sample cost to the person from whom it is taken at the usual public sale rate [38]; (2) calling one or more persons to be present and obtaining their signatures [43]; (3) giving written notice to the food business operator before destroying perishable food unfit for consumption [39]; and (4) following the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, as far as possible [40].
Caveats: The exact identity of persons required to be present under Section 38(7) is not specified.; Whether the CrPC compliance under Section 38(5) applies to all sampling activities or only searches is unclear..

question: Under the FSS Act 2006, what role does the Food Analyst play in the analysis and prosecution of food samples?

C-O3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, the **Food Analyst** plays a crucial role in both the **analysis of food samples** and the **prosecution process**:

### 1. **Analysis of Food Samples**
- A **purchaser** of any article of food (other than a Food Safety Officer) can have the sample **analysed by the Food Analyst** upon payment of prescribed fees [Source 92].
- The Food Analyst must **submit a report of analysis** within a specified period as per regulations [Source 92].
- If the Food Analyst finds the sample **in contravention** of the Act, rules, or regulations, they must **forward the report** along with the analysis report to the relevant authority [Source 93].
- The Food Authority may notify **accredited laboratories** to carry out analysis by Food Analysts [Source 94].
- The Food Authority also establishes or recognises **referral food laboratories** for handling functions under the Act [Source 95].
- Regulations specify the **procedure for submitting samples**, the **form of laboratory reports**, and the **fees payable** [Source 98].

### 2. **Role in Prosecution**
- When a sample is received **under Section 40**, the Food Analyst must send a copy of the **analysis report**—indicating the method of sampling and analysis—to:
  - The **purchaser** of the food article, and
  - The **Designated Officer** [Source 100].
- This report becomes part of the evidence used in **prosecution proceedings** initiated by the Designated Officer [Source 83][Source 85].

In summary, the **Food Analyst** is responsible for conducting or overseeing the **scientific analysis of food samples**, submitting formal reports, and ensuring that findings are communicated to both the complainant and the **Designated Officer**, thereby enabling the **prosecution process** under the Act.

D2.answer: Under the FSS Act 2006, the Food Analyst plays a pivotal role in the analysis and prosecution of food samples. The Food Analyst analyses food samples submitted by purchasers (other than Food Safety Officers) upon payment of fees and issues a report of analysis within a period specified by regulations [92]. If the Food Analyst finds the sample in contravention of the Act, rules, or regulations, the Food Analyst forwards the report to the Designated Officer [93]. The Food Authority notifies accredited laboratories and research institutions for carrying out analysis of samples by Food Analysts [94]. Upon receiving the Food Analyst's report, the Commissioner of Food Safety communicates the decision to the Designated Officer and the concerned Food Safety Officer, who shall launch prosecution before courts of ordinary jurisdiction or Special Court [85]. Thus, the Food Analyst's analysis and reporting are integral to initiating prosecution under the Act.

D3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, the Food Analyst plays a critical role in the analysis and prosecution of food samples by analyzing samples submitted by purchasers on payment of fees, issuing reports of analysis within periods specified by regulations, and forwarding reports to the Designated Officer when contraventions of the Act are found, thereby initiating the prosecution process under Section 42.
Caveats: The exact period within which the Food Analyst must issue the report of analysis is not specified in the provided evidence.; The specific criteria for accreditation of laboratories under Section 40(3) are not detailed in the provided evidence..

question: Under the FSS Act 2006, who is the Designated Officer, and what is that officer's role in the enforcement and adjudication process?

C-O3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, the **Designated Officer** is the **Adjudicating Officer**, who is appointed by the State Government. Specifically, Section 68(1) of the FSS Act 2006 states that for the purposes of adjudication, an officer not below the rank of **Additional District Magistrate** of the district where the alleged offence is committed shall be notified by the State Government as the **Adjudicating Officer** [85].

### Role of the Adjudicating Officer in Enforcement and Adjudication:

1. **Inquiry and Penalty Imposition**:  
   The Adjudicating Officer conducts an inquiry after giving the person a reasonable opportunity for making representation. If satisfied that the person has committed a contravention of the provisions of the Act or the rules/regulations, the officer imposes such penalty as deemed fit [86].

2. **Civil Court Powers**:  
   The Adjudicating Officer is vested with the powers of a civil court. All proceedings before the officer are deemed to be judicial proceedings under Sections 193 and 228 of the Indian Penal Code, and the officer is deemed to be a court for the purposes of Sections 345 and 346 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 [88][89].

3. **Appeals**:  
   Appeals against the orders of the Adjudicating Officer lie to the **Food Safety Appellate Tribunal**, as established under Section 70 of the Act [91].

Thus, the Designated Officer (Adjudicating Officer) plays a central role in enforcing the FSS Act by conducting inquiries, imposing penalties, and exercising judicial powers, with appeals being heard by the designated appellate tribunal.

D2.answer: Under the FSS Act 2006, the Designated Officer is the adjudicating officer appointed by the Central Government, who must be an officer not below the rank of Deputy Secretary to the Government of India or Deputy Secretary to the State Government [1]. The officer's role in enforcement and adjudication includes holding inquiries, summoning persons and requiring production of documents relevant to the case [3], and imposing penalties under sections 4, 5, 5A and 5B after giving the person a reasonable opportunity of being heard [9]. Appeals against the officer's orders lie to the Executive Director within sixty days [10], and penalties imposed may be recovered as an arrear of land revenue [14].

D3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, the Designated Officer is the adjudicating officer appointed by the Central Government, who must be an officer not below the rank of Deputy Secretary to the Government of India or Deputy Secretary to the State Government. The officer's role includes holding inquiries, summoning persons and documents, imposing penalties under sections 4, 5, 5A and 5B after giving a reasonable opportunity of being heard, and the penalties imposed are recoverable as an arrear of land revenue. Appeals against the officer's orders lie to the Executive Director within sixty days.
Caveats: The exact usage of the term 'Designated Officer' in the Act is not found; the Act refers to the officer as 'adjudicating officer'.; The specific manner of inquiry and penalty imposition is to be prescribed by the Central Government..

Under Section 32 of the FSS Act 2006, an improvement notice served on a food business operator must state the following:

4. **A requirement that the food business operator take those measures, or measures which are at least equivalent to them, within a reasonable period (not being less than fourteen days) as may be specified in the notice** [25]

These requirements are outlined in subsection (1) of Section 32, which authorizes the Designated Officer to serve an improvement notice when there are reasonable grounds to believe a food business operator has failed to comply with applicable regulations [21].

question: Under the FSS Act 2006, what is a prohibition order, and what is its legal effect on a food business operator?

C-O3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, a **prohibition order** is an order issued by a court under **Section 33** when a food business operator is convicted of an offence under the Act and the court is satisfied that a health risk exists with respect to that food business [53][54][55].

### Legal Effect of a Prohibition Order:
1. **Imposition of Prohibitions**:  
   The court may impose one or more of the following prohibitions [55]:
   - A prohibition on the use of the **process or treatment** for the purposes of the food business [56].
   - A prohibition on the use of the **premises or equipment** for the purposes of the food business, or any other food business of the same class or description [56].
   - A prohibition on the use of the **premises or equipment** for the purposes of **any food business** [57].

2. **Participation in Management**:  
   The court may also prohibit the food business operator from **participating in the management of any food business**, or any food business of a class or description specified in the order [58].

3. **Enforcement and Publication**:  
   The concerned Food Safety Officer must **serve a copy of the order** on the food business operator and, in the case of an order under subsection (1), **affix a copy at a conspicuous place** on the premises used for the food business [59][60]. Knowingly contravening such an order is an offence punishable with a fine up to **three lakh rupees** [61].

4. **Lifting the Prohibition**:  
   A prohibition order **ceases to have effect** when the court is satisfied, on an application by the food business operator (not earlier than six months after the order), that sufficient measures have been taken to justify lifting the order [65]. The court may also issue a **certificate** confirming compliance, subject to approval by the Designated Officer [62][63][64].

5. **Appeal**:  
   Any person aggrieved by the order may **appeal to the Commissioner of Food Safety**, whose decision is final [48].

Thus, a prohibition order legally restrains the food business operator from carrying out specific activities related to their food business and may lead to suspension or cancellation of their licence if not complied with [43][44].

D2.answer: Under the FSS Act 2006, a prohibition order is an order issued under Section 33, imposed by a court upon conviction of a food business operator and satisfaction that a health risk exists with respect to that food business [54][55][70]. Its legal effect includes prohibiting the use of processes, premises, or equipment for the food business or any other food business of the same class or description, or any food business at all, and prohibiting the operator from participating in the management of any food business [56][57][58]. The order must be served on the operator and affixed at a conspicuous place on the premises, and knowingly contravening it is punishable with a fine which may extend to three lakh rupees [60][61]. The order can be lifted upon application by the operator showing sufficient measures have been taken, subject to certification by the concerned Food Safety Officer with approval of the Designated Officer, and the court may give directions on such applications within specified time limits [62][65][66][67][68].

D3.answer:
A prohibition order under Section 33 of the FSS Act, 2006 is an order issued by a court, upon conviction of a food business operator and satisfaction that a health risk exists, imposing restrictions such as prohibiting the use of processes, premises, equipment, or participation in the management of food businesses. Its legal effect includes mandatory service and affixation of the order, prohibition of specified activities, punishment for contravention, and the possibility of being lifted upon application showing sufficient remedial measures within prescribed time limits.
Caveats: The exact scope of 'sufficient measures' required for lifting the order is not detailed in the provided evidence.; The specific procedures for the court to follow when imposing the order are not fully elaborated..

question: Under the FSS Act 2006, what distinguishes an emergency prohibition notice/order from an ordinary prohibition order?

C-O3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, the distinction between an **emergency prohibition notice/order** and an **ordinary prohibition order** lies in their **triggering conditions, issuing authority, procedural requirements, and consequences**:

### 1. **Ordinary Prohibition Order (Section 33)**  
- **Trigger**: Issued by a **court** when a food business operator is **convicted of an offence** under the Act and the court is **satisfied that a health risk exists** with respect to that food business [79][80].  
- **Authority**: Imposed by the **court**, not an administrative authority [80].  
- **Notice**: The order must be **served on the food business operator**, and a copy **affixed at a conspicuous place** on the premises [84][85].  
- **Consequence of Violation**: Knowingly contravening the order is punishable with a **fine up to three lakh rupees** [85].  
- **Lifting**: Can be lifted by the court upon application by the operator, subject to conditions [89][90].

### 2. **Emergency Prohibition Notice/Order (Section 34)**  
- **Trigger**: Issued by the **Designated Officer** when they are **satisfied that a health risk condition exists** with respect to any food business [95].  
- **Authority**: The **Designated Officer** issues the notice and applies to the **Commissioner of Food Safety** for the order [95][96].  
- **Notice Requirement**: The Designated Officer **must serve notice at least one day before** applying for the order [97].  
- **Order**: The **Commissioner of Food Safety** imposes the prohibition by an order [96].  
- **Consequence of Violation**: Knowingly contravening the order is punishable with **imprisonment up to two years and/or fine up to two lakh rupees** [100].  
- **Lifting**: Ceases to have effect upon the **Designated Officer issuing a certificate** that sufficient measures have been taken [101][102].

### Key Distinctions:
| Aspect | Ordinary Prohibition Order (Sec. 33) | Emergency Prohibition Order (Sec. 34) |
|--------|--------------------------------------|---------------------------------------|
| **Authority** | Court | Designated Officer + Commissioner of Food Safety |
| **Trigger** | Conviction + health risk | Health risk condition (no conviction required) |
| **Prior Notice** | Not specified | At least one day before application [97] |
| **Punishment for Violation** | Fine up to ₹3 lakh [85] | Imprisonment up to 2 years + fine up to ₹2 lakh [100] |
| **Lifting Authority** | Court | Designated Officer |

These distinctions reflect the **urgency and administrative nature** of emergency orders versus the **judicial and post-conviction nature** of ordinary prohibition orders [78][95][96].

D2.answer: Under the FSS Act 2006, an emergency prohibition notice/order under section 34 is distinguished from an ordinary prohibition order under section 33 in several key respects: (1) an ordinary prohibition order can only be imposed after a food business operator is convicted of an offence under the Act and the court is satisfied that a health risk exists [78]-[80], whereas an emergency prohibition notice and order may be issued by the Designated Officer and Commissioner of Food Safety upon satisfaction that a health risk condition exists, without awaiting a conviction [95]-[96]; (2) before applying for an emergency prohibition order, the Designated Officer must serve notice of intention on the food business operator at least one day prior to the application [97]; (3) an emergency prohibition order is lifted upon a certificate from the Designated Officer that sufficient measures have been taken [101], while an ordinary prohibition order is lifted upon court satisfaction, not less than six months after the order [89]. Thus, the emergency regime is a pre-conviction, administrative measure triggered by a health risk condition, while the ordinary regime is a post-conviction judicial measure.

D3.answer:
Under the FSS Act 2006, an emergency prohibition notice/order under section 34 is distinguishable from an ordinary prohibition order under section 33 primarily because the emergency regime does not require a prior conviction of the food business operator and may be triggered by the Designated Officer's satisfaction that a health risk condition exists, whereas an ordinary prohibition order under section 33 can only be imposed after a court convicts the food business operator and is satisfied that a health risk exists. Additionally, the emergency regime requires at least one day's notice of intention before applying for the order, and the order is lifted upon a Designated Officer certificate, while the ordinary order is lifted upon court satisfaction not less than six months after the order.

question: Under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 (as amended), what obligation does an 'extended producer' have, and how was single-use plastic affected by the 2022 amendments?

C-O3.answer:
Based on the provided context, here are the answers:

**Obligation of an 'Extended Producer':**

Under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 (as amended), an "extended producer" (specifically referred to as Producer, Importer, and Brand Owner) has the obligation to fulfill **Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR)** for plastic packaging waste. This includes:

1.  **Registration:** They must register through the centralized online portal developed by the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) [Source 105, Source 169].
2.  **Action Plan:** They must submit an Action Plan containing information on the EPR Target, category-wise, through the centralized portal, along with their registration or renewal application [Source 105, Source 169].
3.  **EPR Targets:** They must meet category-wise EPR targets, which are determined as a percentage of their eligible quantity (Q1, Q2, Q3) of plastic packaging introduced into the market. The targets increase over time: 25% (2021-22), 70% (2022-23), and 100% (2023-24) [Source 105, Source 244, Source 255, Source 262].
4.  **Specific Obligations:** These include obligations for:
    *   **Reuse:** Minimum reuse targets for Category I rigid plastic packaging [Source 155, Source 156].
    *   **Recycling:** Minimum levels of recycling (excluding end-of-life disposal) of plastic packaging waste collected under the EPR target, category-wise [Source 158, Source 248, Source 256].
    *   **End-of-Life Disposal:** Ensuring end-of-life disposal only through specified methodologies [Source 159, Source 160, Source 250, Source 258].
    *   **Use of Recycled Plastic Content:** Mandatory use of recycled plastic in plastic packaging, category-wise [Source 161, Source 163, Source 164, Source 251, Source 260].
5.  **Annual Returns:** They must file annual returns on the plastic packaging waste collected and processed towards fulfilling EPR obligations by 30th June of the next financial year [Source 105, Source 169].
6.  **Environmental Compensation:** Non-compliance with EPR targets can lead to the imposition of environmental compensation based on the polluter pays principle [Source 105, Source 126, Source 167, Source 168].

**Effect of Single-Use Plastic by the 2022 Amendments:**

The 2022 amendments significantly expanded the prohibition on single-use plastics. Specifically, the **Plastic Waste Management (Amendment) Rules, 2022** (G.S.R. 522(E), dated 6th July 2022) prohibited the **manufacture, import, stocking, distribution, sale, and use** of the following single-use plastic items, including polystyrene and expanded polystyrene, **with effect from the 1st July, 2022** [Source 12]:

*   **Ear buds with plastic sticks, plastic sticks for balloons, plastic flags, candy sticks, ice-cream sticks, polystyrene (Thermocol) for decoration** [Source 13].
*   **Plates, cups, glasses, cutlery such as forks, spoons, knives, straws, trays, wrapping or packing films around sweet boxes, invitation cards, and cigarette packets, plastic or PVC banners less than 100 micron, stirrers** [Source 14].

Furthermore, the provisions of this prohibition **shall not apply to commodities made of compostable plastic** [Source 15].

D2.answer: Under the Plastic Waste Management Rules, 2016 (as amended), an 'extended producer' (Producer, Importer, or Brand Owner) is obligated to fulfill Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) for plastic packaging waste as per guidelines specified in Schedule-II [105]. This includes category-wise EPR targets (increasing from 25% in 2021-22 to 100% in 2023-24) [244][245][246], obligations for reuse, recycling, use of recycled plastic content, and end-of-life disposal [158][163][160], registration on the centralized CPCB portal [240], and submission of annual returns. The 2022 amendments introduced Schedule-II with detailed EPR guidelines and refined the single-use plastic provisions by maintaining the prohibition on specified single-use plastic commodities (including polystyrene and expanded polystyrene) effective from 1st July, 2022 [12][13][14], while clarifying exemptions for compostable plastics [15] and 100% biodegradable plastics [166].

An 'extended producer' (Producer, Importer, or Brand Owner) is obligated to fulfill Extended Producer Responsibility for plastic packaging waste as per guidelines specified in Schedule-II, which was introduced by the 2022 Amendment Rules (G.S.R. 522(E) dated 6th July, 2022). question: Under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997, how is the standard rent of a premises determined?

C-O3.answer:
Under the West Bengal Premises Tenancy Act, 1997, the standard (fair) rent of a premises is determined based on different criteria depending on the nature and age of the premises:

1. **For premises constructed and let out after 1984**: The fair rent is fixed at **10% of the cost of construction** plus the **market value of the land** at the time of commencement of construction [2].

2. **For premises constructed in or before 1984**:
   - If the tenancy subsists for **20 years or more**, the fair rent is determined by adding to the rent as on 1.7.1976 not more than three times, and then deducting the increase if any, in the manner provided in Schedule III [3].
   - If the tenancy subsists for **10 years or more but less than 20 years**, the fair rent is determined by adding to the rent as on 1.7.1986 not more than two times, and then deducting the increase if any, in the manner provided in Schedule III, or by accepting the existing rent if such rent is more than the increased rent determined according to that Schedule [4][5].

3. **Pending proceedings**: Where any proceeding is pending at the commencement of the Act for fixation of fair rent under the 1956 Act, the rent fixed under the said Act shall be the fair rent under this Act [6].

4. **General provision**: Where none of the above provisions apply, the fair rent shall be such as would be reasonable, having regard to the situation, locality, condition of the premises, amenities provided, and rent payable in respect of similar premises in the locality [13].

Additionally, while calculating market value of the site, only the portion of the site on which the premises was constructed and 60% of the vacant land appurtenant to such premises is taken into account [10]. The fair rent initially fixed is automatically increased by 5% every three years [13].

The Controller fixes fair rent on application per Section 17 [8], and while calculating land market value, only the constructed portion and 60% of vacant land are considered, with excess treated as amenity [10].

question: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when a contract is breached, what is the rule on compensation under Section 73, and how does a 'penalty' clause differ?

C-O3.answer:
Under **Section 73** of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when a contract is breached, the party suffering by such breach is entitled to receive compensation for any **loss or damage** that:

- **Naturally arose** in the ordinary course of things from the breach, or  
- Was **known to both parties** at the time of contracting to be likely to result from the breach.

Importantly, compensation is **not** awarded for **remote or indirect losses** [1].

For example:
- If a seller fails to deliver goods, the buyer can recover the difference between the contract price and the market price at the time of breach [2][4][5].
- If a party incurs extra expenses due to a breach (e.g., arranging alternative transport), they can claim those expenses [3].
- However, **consequential losses** not foreseeable at the time of contract (like loss of a separate contract not communicated to the breaching party) are **excluded** [11][12][18].

---

In contrast, **Section 74** deals with cases where the contract stipulates a **pre-determined sum** or a **penalty clause** in the event of a breach. In such cases:

- The aggrieved party is entitled to **reasonable compensation**, **not exceeding** the amount named or the penalty stipulated, **regardless of whether actual loss is proven** [20].
- The court assesses what is **reasonable** under the circumstances [22][23].
- This provision applies **only** when the contract explicitly names a sum or includes a penal stipulation.

Thus, the key distinction is:
- **Section 73**: Compensation is based on **actual loss** naturally arising from the breach.
- **Section 74**: Compensation is **capped at the agreed sum or penalty**, and actual loss need not be proven.

[1][20]

D2.answer: Under Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when a contract is breached, the aggrieved party is entitled to compensation for loss or damage that naturally arose in the usual course of things from the breach, or which the parties knew at the time of contract to be likely to result from it, but not for remote or indirect loss [1]. A 'penalty' clause, governed by Section 74, differs in that it applies when the contract names a sum to be paid upon breach or contains a stipulation by way of penalty; in such cases, the aggrieved party is entitled to reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or the penalty stipulated, whether or not actual damage is proved [20]. Thus, while Section 73 limits compensation to actual and foreseeable loss, Section 74 caps recovery under a penalty clause at reasonable compensation, preventing the enforcement of punitive amounts [22].

D3.answer:
Under Section 73 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, compensation for breach of contract is limited to loss or damage that naturally arose in the ordinary course of things or was foreseeable at the time of contract, excluding remote or indirect loss. A 'penalty' clause, governed by Section 74, is not a substitute for compensation; it is enforceable only to the extent of reasonable compensation for the actual loss suffered, and not the full stipulated amount, unless it falls within the exception for bail-bonds or public duty instruments.

question: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, is a liquidated-damages clause that names a sum far exceeding the probable loss enforceable, and what relief does the Act grant?

C-O3.answer:
Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a liquidated-damages clause that names a sum far exceeding the probable loss is **not enforceable as a penalty**. Instead, the Act treats such a clause as a stipulation for penalty, governed by **Section 74**.

### Legal Position:
**Section 74** provides that when a contract has been broken and a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of such breach (or any other stipulation by way of penalty), the party complaining of the breach is entitled to receive **reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or the penalty stipulated for**, whether or not actual damage or loss is proved [20].

Thus, even if the named sum is extravagant or unconscionably high compared to the actual or probable loss, the court is not bound to award the full amount. It must assess **reasonable compensation** within the ceiling of the stipulated sum [20][22][23].

### Relief Granted:
The Act grants the injured party the right to claim **reasonable compensation**, which:
- Is **not limited to actual proof of loss** [20],
- But must be **proportionate to the loss suffered** [20][22][23].

Courts are empowered to reduce the awarded amount to a level that is **just and equitable**, based on the extent of actual harm caused by the breach [20][22][23].

### Conclusion:
A liquidated-damages clause naming a sum far exceeding the probable loss is **not enforceable in full**. Under **Section 74**, the aggrieved party may recover only **reasonable compensation**, which shall not exceed the stipulated amount [20][22][23].

D2.answer: Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, a liquidated-damages clause that names a sum far exceeding the probable loss is not fully enforceable as a penalty. Section 74 provides that when a sum is named in the contract as the amount to be paid in case of breach, or the contract contains any other stipulation by way of penalty, the aggrieved party is entitled only to reasonable compensation not exceeding the amount so named or the penalty stipulated for [20]. The court will assess the actual loss or damage caused by the breach, guided by Section 73, which limits compensation to loss or damage that naturally arose in the usual course of things or which the parties knew was likely to result from the breach, excluding remote and indirect loss [1]. Therefore, the clause is enforceable only to the extent of reasonable compensation for the actual loss suffered, and the excess over the probable loss is not recoverable. The relief granted is reasonable compensation not exceeding the named sum, as assessed by the court.

D3.answer:
A liquidated-damages clause that names a sum far exceeding the probable loss is not fully enforceable as a penalty. Under Section 74 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, the aggrieved party is entitled only to reasonable compensation not exceeding the named sum, and the court will assess the actual loss or damage caused by the breach, excluding remote and indirect loss as per Section 73. The clause is enforceable only to the extent of reasonable compensation, and the excess over the actual loss is not recoverable.

question: Under the Companies Act, 2013, what is the significance of Section 188 for a company entering a supply contract with its related parties, and how did the 2013 Act change the approval regime versus the 1956 Act?

**Significance of Section 188 for a company entering a supply contract with its related parties:**

Section 188 of the Companies Act, 2013 governs **related party transactions**, including supply contracts. Under subsection (1), no company shall enter into any contract or arrangement with a related party with respect to matters such as:

- **(a) Sale, purchase or supply of any goods or materials** [Source 6],
- **(d) Availing or rendering of any services** [Source 9],

**except with the consent of the Board of Directors given by a resolution at a meeting of the Board** and subject to such conditions as may be prescribed [Source 5].

Furthermore, for certain specified transactions, **prior approval of the company by a resolution** is required [Source 13]. This means that for supply contracts falling within the scope of Section 188, the company must obtain both **Board-level approval** and, where applicable, **shareholder approval via a resolution**.

Additionally, related party transactions must be reported in the prescribed form [Source 1], and non-compliance attracts penalties—**five lakh rupees for the company and fifty thousand rupees for every defaulting officer** [Source 5].

---

**Change in the approval regime from the 1956 Act to the 2013 Act:**

The **2013 Act introduced a more stringent and structured approval regime** compared to the 1956 Act:

1. **Board Approval Mandatory**: Unlike the 1956 Act, which had a lighter touch, the 2013 Act mandates **prior approval by the Board of Directors through a resolution** for all related party transactions [Source 5].

2. **Shareholder Approval for Certain Transactions**: The 2013 Act requires **prior approval by shareholders through a resolution** for specific categories of related party transactions [Source 13], a feature not as explicitly codified in the 1956 Act.

3. **Audit Committee Oversight**: The 2013 Act empowers the **Audit Committee to give omnibus approval** for related party transactions, subject to prescribed conditions [Source 19], adding another layer of governance oversight.

4. **Disclosure and Transparency Requirements**: The 2013 Act mandates detailed **disclosure of particulars of related party transactions in the prescribed form** [Source 1], enhancing transparency.

5. **Penal Provisions**: The 2013 Act introduces **strict penalties** for non-compliance, including monetary fines for both the company and defaulting officers [Source 5], which were less pronounced under the 1956 Act.

In summary, the 2013 Act significantly **tightened the regulatory framework** around related party transactions by introducing **mandatory Board and shareholder approvals, Audit Committee oversight, enhanced disclosures, and stricter penalties**, unlike the relatively lenient regime under the 1956 Act.

question: Scenario: A food-delivery platform lists a Kolkata eatery. When a customer falls ill, who is liable under the FSS Act and what municipal duty does the platform owe?

C-O3.answer:
Under the FSS Act, 2006, the **eatery** is the **food business operator (FBO)** and is primarily liable for ensuring food safety under Section 26(1) [Source 35]. It must ensure that food satisfies safety requirements at all stages of production, processing, and sale [Source 35], and is prohibited from selling unsafe, sub-standard, or misbranded food [Source 37].

The **delivery platform**, by listing and facilitating the sale of the eatery’s food, may also be considered an FBO involved in **distribution and sale**, attracting liability under Section 26(1) [Source 35] and Section 26(2)(v) [Source 39], which prohibits sale in contravention of the Act or its regulations.

Regarding the **municipal duty**, the **Kolkata Municipal Corporation** has a statutory obligation under Section 470 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, to take measures for preventing or checking the spread of dangerous diseases [Source 142]. Additionally, under Section 476, it can close places where food is sold if a dangerous disease exists or has recently occurred [Source 148].

Thus:
- **Liability**: Primarily on the **eatery** as the FBO; the **platform** may also be liable if it is deemed to be engaged in distribution/sale.
- **Municipal duty**: To prevent disease spread and inspect/seal unsafe food premises under the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980 [Sources 142, 148].

D2.answer: Under the FSS Act, the Kolkata eatery (as food business operator) is primarily liable for ensuring food safety and is prohibited from selling unsafe food under Section 26(1) [35] and Section 26(2) [36]. The municipal duty owed by the platform includes ensuring the eatery obtains proper municipal licence under KMCA Section 435 [75] and adheres to sanitation standards. The Municipal Commissioner has authority to inspect premises under KMCA Section 491 [177], seize unsafe food under Section 443 [82], and close establishments during disease outbreaks under Sections 476 [147] and 477 [147]. The eatery bears primary liability for the customer's illness, while the platform and municipal authorities share responsibility for regulatory compliance and public health protection.

D3.answer:
Under the FSS Act (Food Safety and Standards Act 2006, Section 26), the eatery is primarily liable as a food business operator for ensuring food safety and is prohibited from selling unsafe food. The food-delivery platform may also face liability if it qualifies as a food business operator or distributor under the Act. The municipal duty involves the Kolkata Municipal Corporation's obligation under KMCA Section 490 to take adequate measures for inspection, supervision, regulation and control of premises to ensure proper environmental sanitation, and the Municipal Commissioner's power under Section 491 to inspect premises for sanitary purposes.
Caveats: Whether food-delivery platform itself qualifies as food business operator under FSS Act; Whether municipal licence was obtained by eatery under KMCA Section 435 [75]; Whether inspection was conducted by Municipal Commissioner under KMCA Section 491 [177].

Under the Indian Contract Act, 1872, when a party fails to perform a contractual obligation that constitutes a "condition" (a fundamental term), the other party is entitled to terminate the contract and claim damages [40]. Maintaining a valid FSSAI licence is a condition precedent for operating a food business [25], and thus a fundamental obligation in the franchise agreement. The suspension of the licence represents a failure to perform this essential condition, giving the franchisor the right to terminate.

Under the **Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980**, Section 435(1) [Source 71], **no person shall use or permit to be used any premises for any non-residential purpose without a municipal licence**. Operating a cloud kitchen—even without dine-in or signage—is a **non-residential use of premises** for the purpose of preparing and selling food.
